target: AG1’s claim that alternatives can effectively replace fossil fuels because a few countries already use very high shares of renewables
objection: High-renewable shares in small or favorable cases such as Iceland, Paraguay, Costa Rica, and Norway do not show that alternatives can supply very large fractions of energy in large, fossil-dependent countries; AG2 pointed to the U.S. having never exceeded 20% alternative energy historically as evidence that large-scale replacement is not yet realistic.

target: AG1’s assumption that renewables plus electrification can make fossil fuels unnecessary
objection: Even if renewables grow, large countries still need dependable firm low-carbon capacity to meet demand when variable generation is low, so grid flexibility alone does not eliminate the reliability role fossil fuels currently play.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear can quickly close the firm-power gap and make a fossil-gas bridge unnecessary
objection: Nuclear is too dangerous and ineffective to be relied on as a serious climate solution because major accidents like Fukushima can wipe out carbon-free electricity gains.

target: AG1’s reliance on renewables plus electrification to replace fossil fuels
objection: Real-world high-renewable systems do not prove that firm low-carbon power at scale is inherently feasible in large countries; AG2 argued that the needed firm-capacity gap remains and therefore fossil fuels still have a role as backup.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear’s occasional accidents do not negate its usefulness
objection: A nuclear accident can erase the carbon-free electricity gains from a plant, so nuclear cannot be treated as a dependable low-carbon substitute that makes fossil fuels unnecessary.

target: AG1’s claim that grid flexibility plus nuclear can remove the need for fossil-fuel reliability backup
objection: Nuclear power is fundamentally baseload-oriented and cannot ramp quickly enough to provide the fast, continuous balancing needed when renewables fluctuate in real time, so fossil fuels or another dispatchable source remain necessary.

target: AG1’s broader conclusion that renewables, nuclear, and grid tools together make fossil fuels unnecessary
objection: If nuclear cannot provide the fast balancing needed, then fossil fuels remain required for reliability and the claim that alternatives can fully replace fossil fuels fails.

target: AG1’s reliance on long-duration storage or hydrogen to cover multi-day or seasonal renewable lulls
objection: Hydrogen or other stored energy made from low-carbon electricity loses energy in conversion, so it increases the amount of low-carbon electricity required rather than solving the reliability problem on its own.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear can supply the firm low-carbon electricity needed for electrolysis and long-duration replacement
objection: Nuclear is not a dependable solution because major accidents can eliminate its carbon-free gains, so it cannot be relied on to make fossil fuels unnecessary at scale.

target: AG1’s claim that hydrogen conversion losses do not prevent full fossil replacement
objection: Even if electrification improves efficiency, major fossil uses such as industrial feedstocks and high-temperature heat still need hydrogen or similar molecules, which greatly increases the electricity requirement and makes full replacement harder.

target: AG1’s claim that nuclear can rapidly supply the extra electricity needed for hydrogen and other synthetic fuels
objection: Nuclear cannot be relied on as a dependable source of scalable firm carbon-free electricity, so it does not remove the need for fossil fuels during the transition.

target: AG1’s claim that high-renewable countries prove fossil fuels are not inherently needed as a bridge
objection: The cited countries are not representative of large, variable-renewables-dominated systems and often rely on dispatchable hydropower or geothermal under favorable local conditions, so they do not show that large countries can eliminate the need for firm backup.

target: AG1’s claim that alternative energy portfolios can provide firm low-carbon reliability without fossil fuels
objection: AG2 argued that large countries have not historically scaled alternatives enough to remove fossil backstops, so a bridge fuel is still needed for reliability while alternatives expand.
